lessons.title: Reading a meta-analytic map
body: This is not a picture of a brain at work but a statistical summary of 148 published PET and fMRI studies of five emotions (Wager et al., 2015), built from the peak coordinates those studies reported.

Each voxel holds the model's expected number of activation (population) centres: summed over a region, it gives the expected number of such centres there for studies of fear, not a signal strength or a p-value.
The default cut of 0.001 is the value the authors chose for drawing their figures, not a significance test, and at that cut each emotion map colours a third to over half of the brain (34–55%).
The model counts reported peaks from emotion-versus-comparison contrasts and has no negative values, so this map cannot show decreases; their absence is not a finding.
The studies used varied tasks and stimuli, and regions that are hard to image, such as the brainstem and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, are probably under-represented.
lessons.notice: Move the Display cut slider up from 0.001, then tick "show unthresholded": which regions stay coloured longest?

claims.text: The five emotion maps come from a Bayesian meta-analysis of 148 studies; each map shows the expected number of activation centres per voxel and was thresholded at 0.001 for display only.
The brainstem and ventromedial prefrontal cortex are likely to be under-represented in these results.

lessons.title: Five emotions, one brain
body: All five maps come from the same model and use the same units, so here, and only here, they share one colour scale.

The authors report that regions such as the amygdala, insula, anterior cingulate cortex and brainstem were likely to be active in all five emotions, though with different and meaningful distributions within each region.

In the "Relative to region size" view the amygdala has the highest value for all five emotions (about 8 to 18 times the average density), but this reflects reported peaks in and around it: a small structure's value is easily swung by a few nearby peaks, which the model's spatial spread carries in from neighbouring tissue, and it does not mean that emotion happens there.
The authors also warn that amygdala values for negative emotions may be over-represented because the field has focused on fear.
Every emotion places some intensity in all seven cortical networks, and about 42–48% of each map lies outside the labelled regions, for example in white matter, cerebellum and basal ganglia.
No emotion mapped onto a single cortical network, and an earlier review found no consistent one-region-per-emotion mapping (Lindquist et al., 2012).
lessons.notice: Show fear alone, then add the other four: is any coloured region fear's alone?

claims.text: Emotion categories were not contained within any one region or system, but were represented as configurations across multiple brain networks.

Limbic and paralimbic regions such as the amygdala, insula, anterior cingulate cortex and brainstem were likely to be active in all five emotion categories, though with different and meaningful distributions within each region.
Amygdala activation intensity for negative emotions may be over-represented, given the field's theoretical focus on fear.
No emotion category mapped to any single cortical network; categories differed in their profiles across networks.
A meta-analytic review found no consistent mapping of each emotion to a single brain region.

lessons.title: Fear vs anxiety
body: Anxiety appears here not as a sixth basic emotion but as a contrast with fear.

In the usual research framing, fear is the response to a threat that is present and identifiable; anxiety is a more sustained apprehension about a threat that is uncertain or not yet here, such as waiting for a shock that may or may not come.
The two maps come from different studies with different methods, so they never share a colour scale; compare their network profiles, which show where each map's evidence lies, not how strong it is.

Even the fear map lies mostly outside the amygdala: about 94% of its intensity falls elsewhere ("Share of evidence" view), although relative to its size the amygdala is far denser than, for example, the default mode network (about 18 against about 1, "Relative to region size" view).
Look for parts of the two profiles that are shared and parts that differ, rather than for one region that separates the two states.
lessons.notice: In the "Relative to region size" view, where do the fear and anxiety profiles agree, and where do they part?

claims.text: Emotion categories, fear included, were not contained within any one region or system, but were represented as configurations across multiple brain networks.
A meta-analytic review found no consistent mapping of each emotion to a single brain region.

lessons.title: Memory retrieval and the default mode network
body: Episodic memory retrieval means bringing back a specific past event: what happened, where and when.

Retrieval is generally reported to engage the hippocampus together with regions of the default mode network, such as the posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, medial prefrontal cortex and lateral parietal cortex.
The default mode network is not only a memory network: the emotion meta-analysis describes it as consistently engaged in semantic memory, person perception, imagining the future and emotion.
The hippocampus is small, so judge it in the "Relative to region size" view rather than by the length of its "Share of evidence" bar.
Like every map here, this one is a statistical result with its own method and threshold; read the info panel before reading the colours.
lessons.notice: Is the evidence for retrieval confined to the default mode network or to the hippocampus?

claims.text: The default mode network is consistently engaged during conceptual processes such as semantic memory, person perception and prospection about future events, as well as in emotion.

lessons.title: Fear vs retrieval
body: The amygdala lies just anterior to the hippocampal head in the medial temporal lobe; being neighbours does not mean doing the same thing, and neither structure does only one thing.

The fear map already reaches the hippocampus: relative to its size, the hippocampus holds about 4 times the average density of the labelled regions in the fear profile, second only to the amygdala at about 18 ("Relative to region size" view).

Fear's density in the default mode network is about average for the labelled regions (about 1 in the "Relative to region size" view); that network is generally reported to be engaged during memory retrieval too.
The two maps come from different studies and methods, so compare their profiles, not their colours; the profiles show where the evidence lies, not how strong it is.
Ask whether the two conditions differ in which regions they use at all, or in how their evidence is weighted across the same networks.
lessons.notice: In the "Relative to region size" view, compare the amygdala, hippocampus and default mode bars for fear and for retrieval.

claims.text: The hippocampus was among the regions engaged across emotion categories, and hippocampal profiles helped distinguish fear from anger.
The default mode network is consistently engaged during conceptual processes such as semantic memory, person perception and prospection about future events, as well as in emotion.
